claims.text: A predictive approach using fine-scale descriptors of atomic mass variance, local lattice distortion, and configurational entropy will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than methods using only bulk properties.
Fine-scale descriptors improve predictions because they capture vibrational scattering mechanisms in disordered lattices.
The target high-entropy alloys contain at least five principal metallic elements.
The target alloys have a disordered crystalline structure.
Such high-entropy alloys are typical materials for thermal-insulation applications.
The proposed algorithm uses atomic-mass contrast, bond-stiffness variability, and local-strain-field descriptors to predict phonon transport.
Atomic mass variance and structural strain mediate local lattice disorder and associated vibrational scattering at micro- to nanoscales.
Severe compositional disorder enhances phonon scattering.
Descriptors of compositional disorder and phonon scattering enable more reliable forecasts of low thermal conductivity.
Models based on average bulk properties fail to represent the increased phonon scattering caused by local disorder.
The proposed approach will reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20% relative to conventional methods.
Alloys classified as low-conductivity by the proposed model will have measured phonon thermal conductivities significantly lower than values predicted by baseline models.
The approach is expected to apply predominantly to alloys having at least five elements and pronounced configurational disorder.
The approach may not apply to binary or near-binary alloys because disorder effects are less important in those systems.
Laser flash analysis or time-domain thermoreflectance can be used in the benchmark to determine phonon thermal conductivity.
X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy can assess structural disorder and local lattice strain in the benchmark samples.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant prediction-error reduction of at least 20% over conventional methods will falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of measured conductivities for model-selected alloys to differ significantly from baseline predictions will falsify the hypothesis.
